title: Family Law
objectives: Identify the property items that may be divided between spouses upon marriage breakdown or the end of a civil union.
Calculate, upon marriage breakdown or the end of a civil union, the value of the property to be divided between the spouses.
Identify the rights of common-law and same-sex spouses in respect to each other's property.
Assess the impact of marriage or civil union upon the spouses' rights of ownership of property acquired before or after the marriage or civil union.

guide.heading: Introduction: provincial law and the priority of matrimonial rights
points: Property and civil rights are provincial, so each province has its own family law statutes or matrimonial property regimes, covering division on marriage breakdown or death. Who may marry is set by federal law.

Matrimonial property rights supersede virtually any other property transfer: the spouse's will, survivorship rights on joint property and binding buy-sell agreements cannot be fulfilled until the equalization right is discharged or waived.
Most provincial family law does not cover common-law or same-sex couples' property: the professional should flag this and suggest legal agreements to protect each partner.
Quebec: couples of different or same sex can enter a civil union (Act of June 2002), equivalent to marriage. 'Spouse' includes married and civil union spouses, but not de facto spouses.
Wills can be challenged for failing to provide for a spouse and dependants. In Quebec, freedom of will is absolute, subject to the survival support right and the family patrimony partition rules.

guide.heading: Death of a spouse and the evolution of spousal rights
points: Marriages and civil unions end on death. In Quebec, the survivor first receives the family patrimony share, then any matrimonial regime share (the deceased's share goes into the succession), then the legacies in the will.
A survivor treated unfairly by the will may, under conditions, obtain a compensatory allowance for having contributed to the enrichment of the deceased spouse's estate.
Alan and Alicia: a $500,000 insurance-funded legacy left 'in lieu of' her statutory rights leaves Alicia $100,000 better off than claiming against the $800,000 estate, so she is unlikely to claim.
Originally, at common law, a married woman had no legal personality: her property became her husband's and spouses could not convey property to each other.

Quebec: community of property has not been regulated by the Civil Code since 1970; couples with no contract are in the partnership of acquests (separate property during the marriage, acquests shared at the end).

1989: Quebec's family patrimony law (economic equality of spouses) requires equal division of family patrimony at the end of the union; couples married earlier could opt out by notarized deed before December 31, 1990.
Family law is complex and heavily litigated: refer clients to an experienced family law lawyer, especially where there are prior marriages or children from other unions.

guide.heading: The matrimonial home and the Quebec family residence
points: Matrimonial home: property in which a spouse has an ownership or leasehold interest, ordinarily occupied by the spouses as their family residence; with mixed use, only the residential part counts (Abdul and Sunnum's semi-detached).

Each spouse has an equal right to reside there regardless of ownership; occupancy rights are personal and give no title. A deserting owner can lose occupancy; the custodial parent often keeps the home; Quebec courts can grant temporary use for a fixed period.

Most provinces bar selling or encumbering the home without the other spouse's consent or court approval; a non-owner spouse can register a notice against title. Several matrimonial homes can exist at once, based on use.

Quebec: if the owner disposes of the residence without consent, the other spouse can claim damages, or seek annulment if a declaration of family residence was registered before the transaction. Lenders should get consent and suggest independent legal advice.

A declaration can also cover a rented residence: once the lessor is notified, the leasing spouse cannot sublet without consent. Without mutual consent, spouses cannot dispose of the furniture of the main family residence.

Quebec's protection applies whatever the matrimonial regime. Everywhere, a home brought into the marriage is not excluded if it is the matrimonial home when the marriage ends (Jean and Jeanne, Sudbury).

guide.heading: Matrimonial property legislation on breakdown
points: Provincial regimes are 'deferred' sharing schemes: spouses deal freely with their own property during the marriage; rights of division arise only on death or breakdown.

Mario's yacht, bought with family money, is matrimonial property: Maude has a deferred interest in half its value. Mario can sell it freely during the marriage, but after a breakdown not without her permission or settling her claim.
Quebec: Maude's deferred interest would exist under the partnership of acquests; if the yacht served both spouses as a secondary residence, it might also fall into the family patrimony.

Provincial laws form a patchwork, but nearly all treat marriage as a partnership. Biggest split: the family vs non-family assets model (focused on assets) versus global equalization of net family property (focused on values).
All provinces allow some contracting out if both spouses freely agree, in writing, signed and witnessed. Only a few give common-law spouses cohabitation property rights.

guide.heading: Quebec: renouncing family patrimony and changing regime
points: Family patrimony is mandatory: it cannot be renounced in advance. Since January 1, 1991, any such agreement is null, even if written and signed.
Renunciation, complete or partial, joint or unilateral, is possible only at a divorce judgment, separation from bed and board, nullity of marriage, dissolution of a civil union or death.
Form: before a notary at death, or by judicial declaration approved by a judge; recorded in the Register of Personal and Movable Real Rights within one year, or the partition is deemed accepted.
A renunciation can be annulled for threat, false claims or a mistake about the document; a judge can refuse it if one spouse took advantage and the advantages are significantly disproportionate.
Unlike family patrimony, the matrimonial regime can be chosen or changed before or during the marriage, through a notary (marriage or civil union contract).
Source: Civil Code of Quebec, Book Two 'The Family', articles 365 to 521.19.

guide.heading: Family patrimony: who and what
points: Created July 1, 1989; takes precedence over the matrimonial regime at separation, divorce, annulment or death; applies only to married and civil union spouses, whatever their regime.

Couples married before July 1, 1989 are covered unless they opted out before Dec. 31, 1990, began proceedings before May 15, 1989 without reconciling, or separated before May 15, 1989 and settled the consequences.

Included whatever the acquisition date: family residences (principal or secondary, e.g., cottage or fishing camp, if used by the family), rights of use, furniture and movables serving them, vehicles owned by the spouses and used by the family.
If each spouse owns a vehicle, both are deemed to serve for family travel unless proven otherwise. A leased vehicle is not included.

Included only for the portion accrued during the marriage: retirement plan rights (e.g., RRSPs) and QPP/CPP benefits; QPP benefits received after a spouse's death are excluded; the QPP partition takes effect at retirement.
Excluded: fixed income securities, shares and other investments, businesses, rental buildings (except the family's portion), cash and bank accounts, and gifts or inheritances.
During the marriage the owner manages family patrimony assets freely, except for restrictions on the family residence and its furniture. Duplex: only the unit the family occupies is included.

guide.heading: Family patrimony: calculating the partition
points: Partition occurs on a judgment of separation as to bed and board, divorce or annulment, or at death. The net value is partitioned, not the assets themselves.

Partitionable value = market value - debts incurred to acquire, improve, maintain or preserve the assets - net value at marriage of assets already owned (plus a share of their increase) - gift or inheritance contributions (plus a share of their increase).
Increase to deduct for an asset owned at marriage = net value at marriage x increase since marriage / gross value at marriage (same logic for a gift or inheritance contribution).
Course answer (Louise): a house owned fully paid before the marriage leaves nothing to divide, since both its value at marriage and its gain since are deducted.

The spouse with the larger net value pays the other (or the estate) half the difference, in cash or assets. The court may order an unequal partition, or exclude QPP/CPP, if equal partition would be unfair.
Partition matters most under separation as to property, since the partnership of acquests and community of property already share most assets acquired during the marriage.

guide.heading: Matrimonial regimes
points: Every couple has a regime governing their finances from the wedding (or civil union) until divorce, separation as to bed and board, dissolution, annulment or death. It can be chosen or changed by contract before or during the union.
No contract: married before July 1, 1970, community of property; after that date, partnership of acquests. Family patrimony is not a regime.

Partnership of acquests: private = owned before the marriage or inherited during it; acquests = everything else acquired during it (wages, income from work or investments). Each manages his or her own; at the end each gets half the other's acquests.
Separation as to property: only private property; each spouse keeps, manages and preserves his or her own assets.

Community of property: legal regime until 1970, no longer regulated by the Civil Code but still binding on couples under it and available by notarized contract; most assets are common, and each keeps private property plus half the common property.
The two principal regimes in Quebec today: partnership of acquests and separation as to property. Liquidation of the regime starts only once the family patrimony has been partitioned.

guide.heading: Gifts: inter vivos and mortis causa
points: A gift contract commits the donor as soon as it is signed, for a transfer then or at a later date. Two types: inter vivos and mortis causa.
Inter vivos: donor and donee both alive; the donor becomes a debtor immediately; irrevocable (no right to cancel) and it survives separation or divorce.

Quebec: a bankrupt generally cannot make or receive gifts in the period before bankruptcy; a donor with a terminal illness cannot validly make an inter vivos gift, though it could be valid if he or she recovers within three years.
Mortis causa: made in anticipation of death; the donor becomes a debtor only at death (the liquidator pays); valid only in a marriage or civil union contract or a will; in theory always revocable.
A mortis causa clause in a marriage contract can be changed by will (Roger's sugar shack) unless the contract made it irrevocable, in which case the spouse's consent is needed.

Divorce, annulment or dissolution revokes mortis causa gifts (unless otherwise provided) but not inter vivos gifts; an inter vivos gift conditional on, e.g., a 10th anniversary fails if divorce comes first.
Marriage contract gift clauses benefit only the spouses and their respective or common children, including those to be born; gifts to a spouse are added to family patrimony and regime rights.

guide.heading: Property rights of common-law spouses
points: Rights vary by province; most, including Quebec, give common-law spouses no property rights: each remains sole owner of what he or she acquired before or during cohabitation.
Some provinces allow support claims between common-law partners, and a few include same-sex couples.
Couples of any gender may sign a cohabitation agreement (a contract), which the courts will enforce on request.
Without an agreement, the claimant must show a financial or deemed contribution, proving unjust enrichment of the other or a tacit partnership; cohabitation alone does not justify sharing.
Quebec: de facto couples (including same-sex couples) can enter a civil union to obtain the same property and support rights as married spouses.

guide.heading: Tutorship to minors in Quebec
points: Majority is 18. A minor cannot exercise civil rights unless emancipated: from 16, emancipation allows simple administration acts only; full administration acts (e.g., selling an immovable) need full emancipation by the court.
Legal tutorship: the parents act together without any court appointment; if one dies, the other continues alone.

Minor's assets over $25,000: legal tutors must set up a three-member tutorship council (chosen by a meeting of relatives), make an inventory, take out an insurance bond and invest per the Civil Code list; the council authorizes loans and sales.

Dative tutorship: tutor designated by both parents (will or mandate) or appointed by the court when the parents die or are stripped of authority; may be limited to the property. A three-person council is always required; bond if over $25,000.
If no one can act, the director of youth protection becomes tutor to the person and the Public Curator tutor to the property.
The Public Curator oversees all dative tutors and the legal tutors managing over $25,000, audits their annual accounts and charges fees to the minor's estate.

guide.heading: Union abroad
points: Generally, the matrimonial regime of a couple married abroad is set by the law in force where and when they married.
In certain cases the applicable law is that of the first common domicile, the last common domicile or, failing which, the place of celebration.
Maria and Mario married in Italy and moved to Canada ten years later: Italian law governs their regime, but Quebec's family patrimony rules have priority and apply to all couples.

Lise and Benoit, Quebecers who married in Jamaica: their common domicile was Quebec, so the Civil Code applies and they are under the partnership of acquests. Consult an expert in international cases.

guide.heading: Planning scenario and worked examples
points: Manuel and Maria (Quebec, no contract): the house in Manuel's name, acquired after the marriage and used as the family residence, is split equally under family patrimony; her honeymoon waiver is null. The family cars are shared too.

Regime = partnership of acquests: Manuel's tools are excluded; the business van (half paid from Maria's salary) is not family patrimony but is an acquest; the daughter's golf cart is not the spouses' property.

Jeanne and Henri (course answer): her pre-owned home nets $0; his RRSP $30,000 + furniture $15,000 - $15,000 debt = $30,000, so he owes her $15,000. Her $10,000 saved during marriage is an acquest; she repays half the $5,000 trip debt.
Dupuis (Appendix A): Joseph's house had a $13,000 net value at marriage; increase deducted = $13,000 x $80,000 / $40,000 = $26,000. Marie deducts the car and furniture bought with her inheritance.
Dupuis result: family patrimony Joseph $183,000, Marie $20,000; $101,500 each, so Joseph pays $81,500. Joseph's leased minivan is excluded.

Then the partnership of acquests: Marie's $54,000 of inheritance-funded bonds and savings are private; Joseph's shares ($28,000) and bank account ($4,000) are $32,000 of acquests, half of which goes to Marie.

tips: EXAM TIP: Family patrimony is not a matrimonial regime. Quebec couples married after 1970 without a contract are in the partnership of acquests.
EXAM TIP: Family patrimony can't be renounced in advance, only at divorce, separation from bed and board, nullity or death, and it must be registered within a year.
EXAM TIP: Quebec order: family patrimony first, then the matrimonial regime, then (at death) the will or the intestacy rules.
DID YOU KNOW? A leased car is not family patrimony: only vehicles owned by the spouses and used by the family count.
EXAM TIP: Mortis causa gifts are revocable and fall on divorce; inter vivos gifts are irrevocable and survive divorce.
DID YOU KNOW? Legal tutors need a tutorship council once the child's assets top $25,000; dative tutors always need one.
EXAM TIP: The net VALUE of family patrimony is split, not the assets: the richer spouse pays half the difference in cash or property.
DID YOU KNOW? Living together gives Quebec de facto spouses no property rights; a civil union gives them the same rights as marriage.
EXAM TIP: Shares, businesses, cash and bank accounts are outside family patrimony, but under the partnership of acquests they may still be shared.

flashcards.front: Priority of matrimonial property rights
flashcards.back: They supersede virtually any other property transfer: the spouse's will, survivorship rights on jointly owned property and binding buy-sell agreements cannot be fulfilled until the equalization right is discharged or waived.

flashcards.front: Quebec: limits on the content of a will
flashcards.back: A person has absolute liberty on the content of his or her will, subject only to the survival support right and the rules on partition of family patrimony assets.

flashcards.front: Quebec: compensatory allowance
flashcards.back: A surviving spouse who feels unfairly treated in the will may, under certain conditions, receive a compensatory allowance for having contributed to the enrichment of the deceased spouse's estate.

flashcards.front: Legacy 'in lieu of' matrimonial rights (Alan and Alicia)
flashcards.back: Leave the spouse a legacy (e.g., funded by life insurance) stated to be in lieu of her rights under provincial legislation and worth more than her claim; she is better off accepting it and unlikely to make a claim.

flashcards.front: 1989 Quebec family patrimony law: purpose
flashcards.back: To support the economic equality of spouses: marriage and civil union are treated as an economic association, with an equal division of the family patrimony when the union ends.

flashcards.front: Matrimonial home (definition)
flashcards.back: Property in which a spouse has an ownership or leasehold interest and that the spouses ordinarily occupy as their family residence. With mixed use, only the part used as the family residence.

flashcards.front: Non-owner spouse's occupancy rights
flashcards.back: Equal right to reside regardless of ownership; personal against the other spouse, giving no title. A deserting owner can lose occupancy temporarily; the custodial parent often gets it; Quebec courts can grant 'temporary use' for a fixed period.

flashcards.front: Quebec: declaration of family residence
flashcards.back: Registered by the non-owner spouse at the land registry office. Without it, a sale or mortgage made without consent gives a claim for damages; if registered before the transaction, the spouse can seek its annulment.

flashcards.front: Quebec: family residence that is rented
flashcards.back: A declaration can be made when only one spouse is on the lease; once the lessor is notified, the leasing spouse cannot sublet without the other spouse's consent.

flashcards.front: 'Deferred' sharing of matrimonial property
flashcards.back: Spouses deal freely with their own property during the marriage; the other spouse's right to share arises only on death or marriage breakdown (e.g., Mario may sell his yacht during the marriage).

flashcards.front: Two models of provincial matrimonial property law
flashcards.back: The family assets vs non-family assets model (focused on particular assets) and the global equalization of net family property approach (focused on values).

flashcards.front: Contracting out of a matrimonial property regime
flashcards.back: Permitted in all provinces (some more than others) if both spouses freely agree, in writing, signed and witnessed. In Quebec, family patrimony can only be renounced when the union ends.

flashcards.front: Quebec: when can family patrimony be renounced?
flashcards.back: Only at a divorce judgment, separation from bed and board, nullity, dissolution of a civil union or death, completely or partially, jointly or unilaterally. Advance renunciation has been null since January 1, 1991.

flashcards.front: Quebec: formalities to renounce family patrimony
flashcards.back: Before a notary (at death) or by judicial declaration approved by a judge; recorded in the Register of Personal and Movable Real Rights within one year, failing which the partition is deemed accepted.

flashcards.front: Quebec: when can a renunciation be annulled or refused?
flashcards.back: Annulled if made under threat or false claims, or by mistake about the document's nature. A judge can refuse it if one spouse took advantage of the other and the advantages are significantly disproportionate.

flashcards.front: Quebec: changing the matrimonial regime during the marriage
flashcards.back: Allowed: the spouses meet a notary to dissolve the current regime and draft or modify a marriage (or civil union) contract.

flashcards.front: Quebec civil union: rights shared with married spouses
flashcards.back: Since June 2002: family residence protection, family patrimony, compensatory allowance, recognition as successor on intestacy, mutual support (collected by Revenu Quebec). De facto spouses are excluded.

flashcards.front: Quebec family property: key dates
flashcards.back: July 1, 1970: acquests becomes the default regime. May 15, 1989: proceedings/separation cut-off. July 1, 1989: family patrimony starts. Dec. 31, 1990: opt-out deadline. Jan. 1, 1991: advance waivers null. June 2002: civil unions.

flashcards.front: Family patrimony: scope
flashcards.back: Has precedence on separation, divorce, annulment or death; mandatory for couples married after July 1, 1989, whatever their regime; applies to married and civil union spouses only.

flashcards.front: Couples married before July 1, 1989 escape family patrimony if they...
flashcards.back: Renounced it before December 31, 1990; began proceedings before May 15, 1989 without reconciling; or stopped living together before May 15, 1989 and settled the consequences of their separation.

flashcards.front: Family patrimony: included whatever the acquisition date
flashcards.back: Family residences (principal or secondary, if used by the family), rights of use of them, furniture and movables serving them, and vehicles owned by the spouses and used by the family (if each owns one, both are presumed).

flashcards.front: Family patrimony: included only if accrued during the marriage
flashcards.back: Rights in a retirement plan and QPP/CPP benefits accrued during the marriage (QPP benefits acquired following a spouse's death are excluded). QPP: the right to partition takes effect at retirement.

flashcards.front: Events that trigger family patrimony partition
flashcards.back: A judgment of separation as to bed and board, divorce or annulment of the marriage, or the death of a spouse.

flashcards.front: Family patrimony: deductions from market value
flashcards.back: Debts incurred to acquire, improve, maintain or preserve the assets; net value at marriage of assets already owned plus a share of their increase; gift or inheritance contributions plus a share of their increase.

flashcards.front: Court's discretion in a family patrimony partition
flashcards.back: It may order an unequal partition if an equal one would be unfair and, for the same reason, order that QPP and CPP benefits not be partitioned.

flashcards.front: Increase-in-value deduction for an asset owned at marriage
flashcards.back: Net value at marriage x increase (or decrease) in value since marriage / gross value at marriage. Dupuis house: $13,000 x $80,000 / $40,000 = $26,000.

flashcards.front: Assets excluded from family patrimony
flashcards.back: Fixed income securities, shares and other investments; businesses; rental buildings (except the family's own portion); cash and bank accounts; gifts and inheritances. They may still be shared under the regime.

flashcards.front: Quebec default regime by marriage date
flashcards.back: Married before July 1, 1970: community of property. Married (or in a civil union) after that date: partnership of acquests.

flashcards.front: Partnership of acquests
flashcards.back: Private: assets owned before the marriage and inheritances received during it. Acquests: everything else acquired during the marriage (wages, income from work or investments). At the end, each gets half the other's acquests.

flashcards.front: Separation as to property
flashcards.back: Only private property, no acquests: each spouse owns, manages and keeps his or her own assets. Family patrimony partition has its biggest impact under this regime.

flashcards.front: Community of property
flashcards.back: Legal regime until 1970; no longer regulated by the Civil Code but still binds couples under it; can be chosen by notarized contract. Most assets are common; at the end each keeps private property and half the common property.

flashcards.front: Quebec: furniture of the main family residence
flashcards.back: Without mutual consent, the spouses cannot dispose of the furniture used by the couple in the main family residence, whatever their matrimonial regime.

flashcards.front: Inter vivos gift vs gift mortis causa
flashcards.back: Inter vivos: donor and donee alive; irrevocable; survives divorce. Mortis causa: in anticipation of death; only in a marriage or civil union contract or a will; revocable; revoked by divorce unless otherwise provided.

flashcards.front: Quebec: inter vivos gift by a terminally ill donor
flashcards.back: Not valid under the Civil Code, but it could become valid if the donor recovers within three years.

flashcards.front: Who can benefit from gift clauses in a marriage contract?
flashcards.back: Only the spouses and the children of the spouses (respective or common), including children to be born. Gifts to a spouse are added to family patrimony and regime entitlements.

flashcards.front: Common-law partner's property claim without an agreement
flashcards.back: Cohabitation alone is not enough: the claimant must prove a financial or deemed contribution, i.e., that the other was unjustly enriched or that there was a tacit partnership.

flashcards.front: Quebec: age of majority and emancipation
flashcards.back: Majority at 18. From 16, a minor can be emancipated, allowing simple administration acts only. Full administration acts (e.g., selling an immovable) need full emancipation by the court.

flashcards.front: Legal tutorship (Quebec)
flashcards.back: The parents are tutors without court appointment; the survivor continues alone. Over $25,000 of assets: tutorship council of 3, inventory, insurance bond, Civil Code investment list; the council authorizes loans and sales.

flashcards.front: Dative tutorship (Quebec)
flashcards.back: Tutor designated by both parents (will or mandate) or appointed by the court; may be for the property only. A tutorship council of 3 is always required; inventory, annual reports, bond if the property exceeds $25,000.

flashcards.front: Quebec: no one available to act as dative tutor
flashcards.back: The director of youth protection is normally appointed tutor to the person, and the Public Curator tutor to the property.

flashcards.front: Quebec Public Curator: role with tutors
flashcards.back: Oversees all dative tutors and the legal tutors managing more than $25,000; audits their reports, receives their annual accounts and charges fees to the minor's estate.

flashcards.front: Quebec tutorship: key numbers
flashcards.back: 16: emancipation possible. 18: majority. $25,000: legal tutors need a council, inventory and bond, and come under Public Curator oversight. Dative tutors: council and oversight always; bond above $25,000. Councils have 3 members.

flashcards.front: Union abroad: which law sets the matrimonial regime?
flashcards.back: Generally the law where and when they married; in certain cases, the first common domicile, the last common domicile or, failing that, the place of celebration. Quebec family patrimony still applies first.

flashcards.front: General principle of family property law
flashcards.back: Each spouse keeps the value of the property owned at the start of the union; the net value of property acquired during the relationship is divided, subject to the matrimonial regime.

flashcards.front: Can a couple have more than one matrimonial home?
flashcards.back: Yes, at the same time, based on use. Protection against unilateral dealings may be in matrimonial property law or in separate 'homestead' legislation.

flashcards.front: How a family patrimony partition is balanced
flashcards.back: The spouse with the greater net value compensates the other (or the other's estate) by a cash payment or a transfer of assets of like value.

flashcards.front: Savings bonds bought during the marriage (partnership of acquests)
flashcards.back: Excluded from family patrimony, but partitioned as acquests; if funded by an inheritance (like Marie's), they are private property instead.

flashcards.front: Leased vehicle and the family patrimony
flashcards.back: Not included: only vehicles owned by the spouses and used by the family count (Joseph's rented minivan was left out).

flashcards.front: Dupuis example: equalizing payments
flashcards.back: Family patrimony: Joseph $183,000, Marie $20,000; $203,000 in total, so $101,500 each and Joseph pays Marie $81,500. Then half of his $32,000 of acquests (shares and bank account).

questions.q: Why can a spouse's claim under provincial matrimonial property legislation disrupt a deceased's will, joint ownership arrangements or a buy-sell agreement?
options: A will is automatically revoked once a matrimonial claim is made
Buy-sell agreements are not binding on owners who are married
Matrimonial property rights generally take priority over them
Survivorship rights apply only to joint owners who are unmarried
questions.explain: Rights under matrimonial property legislation supersede virtually any other form of property transfer, including the spouse's will, survivorship rights on joint property and binding buy-sell agreements. Those obligations wait until the equalization right is discharged or waived.

questions.q: Who may legally marry in Canada is determined by provincial law, just like the division of matrimonial property.
options: True
False
questions.explain: Who may marry is determined by federal law. Property and civil rights, including matrimonial property, fall under provincial jurisdiction, which is why each province has its own family property legislation.

questions.q: When a married spouse dies in Quebec leaving a will, in what order does the surviving spouse receive value from the deceased's property?
options: Family patrimony share, matrimonial regime share, then legacies
Legacies under the will, then family patrimony, then the regime
Matrimonial regime share, then legacies, then family patrimony
Family patrimony share, then legacies, then the regime share
questions.explain: The surviving spouse first receives his or her share of the family patrimony, then any share under the matrimonial regime (the deceased's share goes into the succession), and only then the legacies left in the will.

questions.q: Raymond, remarried, wants his $900,000 estate to go to the children of his first marriage. His wife's matrimonial property claim would be worth about $350,000. Which strategy from the course best discourages a claim?
options: Leave her nothing, since a will overrides matrimonial property rights
Hold all his assets jointly with his children with right of survivorship
Sign a buy-sell agreement so his business shares pass to his children
Leave her $450,000, funded by insurance, in lieu of her statutory rights
questions.explain: As with Alan and Alicia, a legacy (here funded by life insurance) stated to be in lieu of her rights under provincial legislation leaves her better off accepting the will, so she is unlikely to claim. Wills, joint ownership and buy-sell agreements all yield to matrimonial claims.

questions.q: Which matrimonial regime applies to a couple who married in Quebec in 2015 without a marriage contract?
options: Community of property
Partnership of acquests
Separation as to property
Family patrimony
questions.explain: Couples married in Quebec without a contract since 1970 are under the partnership of acquests. Family patrimony is not a matrimonial regime: it applies on top of whatever regime the couple has.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a non-owner spouse's rights in the matrimonial home?
options: A half interest in the title once they have lived there a year
No right to stay there if the owner spouse asks him or her to leave
An equal right to live there, personal against the other spouse
A right to sell the home if the owner spouse deserts the family
questions.explain: Each spouse has an equal right to reside in the matrimonial home regardless of ownership. Occupancy rights are personal against the other spouse and give no title; an owner spouse who deserts may even lose occupancy temporarily.

questions.q: Luc, sole owner of the family residence in Laval, sells it without his wife's consent. She had registered a declaration of family residence before the sale. What can she do?
options: Ask the court to annul the sale
Only claim damages; the sale stands
Nothing, since Luc is the sole owner
Claim half the price but not undo it
questions.explain: The Civil Code protects the family residence. A non-owner spouse can claim damages when the owner disposes of it without consent; if a declaration of family residence was registered before the transaction, the spouse can request its annulment.

questions.q: Jeanne owned a house before she married Jean in Ontario. They lived in it throughout the marriage, and it was still their home when the marriage ended. How is it generally treated?
options: As her excluded property, since she owned it before marriage
As shared property only for the years after the wedding
As her own property unless Jean helped pay the mortgage
As the matrimonial home, even though she owned it beforehand
questions.explain: Unlike most property, a residence brought into the marriage by either spouse is not excluded: it is the matrimonial home if it is used as such when the marriage ends.

questions.q: During their marriage, Chris bought a motorboat with family money and registered it in his name. The couple is still happily married. Can Chris sell the boat without his wife's consent?
options: No; she has owned a half share of it since the date of purchase
Yes; her deferred interest has no effect during the marriage
No; assets bought with family money need both signatures
Yes, but he must pay her half the proceeds when he sells
questions.explain: Matrimonial property regimes are deferred-sharing schemes: until death or marriage breakdown, Chris can deal with the boat as sole owner and keep the proceeds. Only after a breakdown would he need her permission or have to settle her equalization claim first.

questions.q: In Quebec, in which situation could a yacht registered in one spouse's name become part of the family patrimony?
options: It was paid for out of the owner's salary
It is worth more than $25,000 at the separation
Both spouses use it as a secondary residence
It was bought after July 1, 1989
questions.explain: Family residences, including secondary residences used by the family, are family patrimony, so a yacht both spouses use as a secondary residence may be included. Bought from salary, it would otherwise be an acquest under the partnership of acquests.

questions.q: In Quebec, at what point can spouses validly renounce the partition of their family patrimony?
options: Only at divorce, separation from bed and board, nullity or death
At any time during the marriage, through a notarized marriage contract
Only before the wedding, in a notarized marriage contract
During the marriage, if each spouse gets legal advice
questions.explain: Since January 1, 1991, spouses cannot renounce in advance; any earlier agreement is null. They can renounce (completely or partially, jointly or unilaterally) only at a divorce judgment, separation from bed and board, nullity, dissolution of a civil union or death.

questions.q: After her husband's death, Ginette renounces the partition of the family patrimony before a notary, but the renunciation is never entered in the Register of Personal and Movable Real Rights. Two years pass. What is the result?
options: The renunciation is valid but cannot bind creditors
The liquidator decides whether partition applies
The family patrimony is shared by the children
She is deemed to have accepted the partition
questions.explain: A renunciation must be recorded in the Register of Personal and Movable Real Rights (Registre des droits personnels et reels mobiliers) within one year of the death or judgment. If it is not, the partition is considered accepted.

questions.q: Which right do Quebec civil union spouses have, the same as married spouses?
options: To automatic joint ownership of each other's assets
To inherit from each other if one dies intestate
To a $200,000 preferential share on an intestacy
To an exemption from the family patrimony rules
questions.explain: Under the 2002 Act instituting civil unions, civil union spouses have married spouses' rights: family residence protection, family patrimony, compensatory allowance, recognition as successor on intestacy and mutual support (collectable by Revenu Quebec).

questions.q: In the Quebec rules on spouses' property, 'spouse' covers married spouses, civil union spouses and de facto spouses who have lived together for at least three years.
options: True
False
questions.explain: In Quebec, 'spouse' includes married and civil union spouses but not de facto (common-law) spouses, whatever the length of cohabitation. De facto couples can enter a civil union to obtain those rights.

questions.q: Which couple married in Quebec before July 1, 1989 is NOT subject to the family patrimony rules?
options: One that chose separation as to property in a 1980 marriage contract
One that renounced the rules in a notarized deed signed in 1993
One that separated before May 15, 1989 and settled the consequences
One with no children and separate bank accounts throughout
questions.explain: Pre-1989 couples are covered unless they renounced before December 31, 1990, began proceedings before May 15, 1989 without reconciling, or stopped living together before May 15, 1989 and settled their separation. The regime is irrelevant and a 1993 renunciation is too late.

questions.q: Which asset is part of the Quebec family patrimony regardless of when it was acquired?
options: A country cottage used by the family on weekends
Shares bought by one of the spouses during the marriage
A rental building owned by one of the spouses
A savings account opened during the marriage
questions.explain: Family residences, principal or secondary (a cottage, country condo or fishing camp used by the family), are included whatever the date of acquisition. Shares, rental buildings (except the family's portion) and bank accounts are excluded.

questions.q: Which asset is included in the Quebec family patrimony only to the extent it was accumulated during the marriage?
options: Furniture used by the family
The principal family residence
Vehicles used by the family
Rights in a retirement plan
questions.explain: Retirement plan rights and QPP/CPP benefits are included only for the portion accrued during the marriage. Residences, their furniture and family vehicles are included whatever the acquisition date (subject to deductions for value brought into the marriage).

questions.q: In Quebec, if each spouse owns a vehicle, both vehicles are deemed to be used for family travel unless there is proof to the contrary.
options: True
False
questions.explain: The course notes this presumption: when each spouse owns a vehicle, both are deemed to serve for family travel, so both fall into the family patrimony unless proven otherwise.

questions.q: How are QPP earnings registered during the marriage treated in a Quebec family patrimony partition?
options: Excluded, since they have no value at the time of the divorce
Split equally, but the right takes effect only at retirement
Paid out in cash to the other spouse on the divorce date
Split equally, including survivor benefits from a prior spouse
questions.explain: QPP earnings registered between the marriage and its end are partitioned equally, but having no value as such at dissolution, they only confer a right to partition that takes effect at retirement. QPP benefits acquired following a spouse's death are excluded.

questions.q: Sylvie owns a duplex in Montreal: her family lives in one unit and the other is rented out. If the marriage ends, how is the duplex treated?
options: All of it is family patrimony, because the family lives in the building
All of it is excluded because it produces rental income
Occupied unit in family patrimony; rented unit under the regime
Rented unit in family patrimony; occupied unit is private
questions.explain: Only the value of the unit the family occupies is part of the family patrimony, as in Paul's duplex example (likewise, only the occupied part of a mixed-use property is a matrimonial home). The rented part is partitioned under the couple's matrimonial regime.

questions.q: On a Quebec family patrimony partition, the assets themselves are divided, with each spouse taking a half interest in each asset.
options: True
False
questions.explain: It is the net value of the family patrimony assets, not the assets themselves, that is partitioned. The spouse with the greater value compensates the other in cash or with property of equal value.

questions.q: Which amount is subtracted from market value when calculating the partitionable value of a Quebec family patrimony?
options: The net value at marriage of a home one spouse already owned
The original cost of furniture bought during the marriage
Mortgage payments made from both salaries during the marriage
The income tax that would be payable if the assets were sold
questions.explain: From market value you deduct debts incurred to acquire, improve, maintain or preserve the assets; the net value at marriage of assets already owned plus a portion of their increase; and gift or inheritance contributions plus a portion of the increase.

questions.q: A Quebec court may order an unequal partition of the family patrimony if it judges that an equal partition would be unfair.
options: True
False
questions.explain: The court has the discretionary power to order an unequal partition when an equal one would be unfair, and for the same reason it can order that QPP and CPP benefits not be partitioned.

questions.q: Which asset is excluded from the Quebec family patrimony?
options: An RRSP accumulated during the marriage
The family's cottage in the Laurentians
Furniture in the principal family residence
A stock portfolio built during the marriage
questions.explain: Fixed income securities, shares and other investments, businesses, rental buildings, cash and bank accounts, and gifts or inheritances are outside the family patrimony, although they may still be divided under the matrimonial regime.

questions.q: Under the partnership of acquests, which asset is private property rather than an acquest?
options: Savings built from one spouse's salary during the marriage
A cottage one spouse inherited during the marriage
Investment income earned by one spouse during the marriage
A car bought with one spouse's wages during the marriage
questions.explain: Private property includes assets owned before the marriage and assets inherited during it. All other assets acquired during the marriage are acquests, including wages and income from investments or work.

questions.q: Ana and Ben, under the partnership of acquests, divorce. Ana saved $40,000 from her salary during the marriage. Ben's only asset is $30,000 in cash he had before the marriage. Ignoring family patrimony, what happens under the regime?
options: Ben owes Ana $15,000, half of his savings
Ana owes Ben $5,000, half of the difference
Ana owes Ben $20,000, half of her acquests
Nothing; each spouse keeps his or her own
questions.explain: On dissolution, each spouse keeps his or her private property and is entitled to half the other's acquests. Ana's salary savings are acquests, so Ben gets $20,000; Ben's pre-marriage cash is private and is not shared.

questions.q: Which statement about Quebec's community of property regime is accurate?
options: It still binds couples married under it and can be chosen by contract
It was abolished in 1989 and all of its couples were converted to acquests
It applies when a couple marries without a contract today
It applies only to civil union spouses who sign no contract
questions.explain: Community of property was the legal regime until 1970 and is no longer regulated by the Civil Code, but couples married under it remain subject to it and new couples can elect it by notarized contract. On dissolution each keeps private property and half the common property.

questions.q: In Quebec, the family residence and its contents are protected for the whole time the spouses live together as a couple, whatever their matrimonial regime.
options: True
False
questions.explain: The family residence protection applies regardless of the matrimonial regime. A non-owner spouse can strengthen it by registering a declaration of family residence, and the spouses cannot dispose of the residence's furniture without mutual consent.

questions.q: Under the Civil Code of Quebec, a donor cannot reserve in the gift contract a right to cancel an inter vivos gift at his or her discretion.
options: True
False
questions.explain: An inter vivos gift is irrevocable: once the contract is signed, the donor is committed (becomes a debtor) and cannot later cancel the gift or decide to sell the asset.

questions.q: In Quebec, where can a gift mortis causa (made in anticipation of death) validly be made?
options: In any written contract signed by the donor before two witnesses
Only in a notarial deed of gift registered on title
In a marriage contract only, but never in a will
Only in a marriage or civil union contract, or in a will
questions.explain: Mortis causa gifts can only be made in a marriage or civil union contract or in a will; anywhere else they are null, a rule meant to avoid imperilling a life. The donor becomes a debtor only at death.

questions.q: Paul's marriage contract leaves his cottage to his wife at his death, with no clause making the gift irrevocable. His later will leaves the cottage to his nephew. Paul dies, still married. Who gets the cottage?
options: The wife; a marriage contract always prevails over a will
The nephew; the will overrides the revocable contract clause
The wife, unless the nephew obtains her written consent
Both, as co-owners in equal shares under the two documents
questions.explain: A mortis causa gift in a marriage contract is, in theory, revocable, so a clause in the donor's will can change it, as in Roger's sugar shack example. Only if the contract had made the gift irrevocable would the spouse's consent be needed.

questions.q: Marc's marriage contract provides (1) $10,000 to each child on his or her 18th birthday and (2) all his personal property to his wife at his death. The couple divorces; the contract says nothing more. What becomes of the two clauses?
options: Only the gift of his property at death remains in force
Both clauses remain in force despite the divorce
Only the $10,000 gifts to the children remain in force
Neither clause survives the divorce
questions.explain: The $10,000 promise is an inter vivos gift, which remains in force regardless of divorce. The gift of property at death is mortis causa and, unless otherwise provided, is revoked by divorce, annulment or dissolution of a civil union.

questions.q: Lucie's marriage contract says she will pay her husband $15,000 on their 15th wedding anniversary. They divorce after eight years of marriage. What is the effect of the clause?
options: Nothing is owed, since the condition can no longer be met
She owes $15,000 now, as an inter vivos gift is irrevocable
She owes $8,000, prorated for the years of marriage
She owes $15,000 on the date the anniversary would fall
questions.explain: It is an inter vivos gift conditional on reaching the 15th anniversary. Such a gift is not revocable, but after the divorce the condition can never be satisfied, so the husband receives nothing.

questions.q: Without a cohabitation agreement, what must a common-law partner generally prove to obtain a share of property held by the other?
options: That they lived together for at least three years
That they had a child together and shared a home
That the property was registered in both their names
Unjust enrichment of the other, or a tacit partnership
questions.explain: Courts have held that cohabitation alone does not justify sharing wealth. The claimant must show a financial or deemed contribution, proving that the other party was unjustly enriched or that there was a tacit partnership between them.

questions.q: In Quebec, de facto (common-law) spouses acquire the same property rights as married spouses after living together for several years.
options: True
False
questions.explain: Quebec gives de facto spouses no property rights based on spousal status; each remains sole owner of what he or she acquired. Couples who want those rights can enter a civil union or sign a cohabitation agreement.

questions.q: Elodie, 17, has been emancipated (not fully) and received a building lot as a gift. She wants to sell it now. What is her situation?
options: She can sell it alone, since her emancipation gives her full legal capacity
She cannot sell yet; selling an immovable is a full administration act
She can sell alone once the Public Curator approves the price
She can sell alone, because gifted property escapes tutorship
questions.explain: From 16, an emancipated minor may perform simple administration acts to preserve her assets. Selling an immovable is a full administration act, which requires full emancipation by the court or reaching majority at 18, as in Mathieu's example.

questions.q: Under legal tutorship in Quebec, when must the parents establish a tutorship council?
options: As soon as the minor receives any gift
When the minor's assets exceed $50,000
When the minor's assets exceed $25,000
Only once one of the parents has died
questions.explain: Parents act as legal tutors without court appointment. Once the minor's assets exceed $25,000, they must set up a tutorship council (usually three members chosen by a meeting of relatives) and, under the Public Curator's supervision, make an inventory and secure the assets.

questions.q: After her sister and brother-in-law die, Nadine is appointed by the court as tutor to their 6-year-old daughter, who inherits $18,000. Which statement is accurate?
options: She is a dative tutor and must have a tutorship council anyway
She is a legal tutor, so no tutorship council is needed below $25,000
The Public Curator itself manages the $18,000 for the child
She needs no supervision since the amount is under $25,000
questions.explain: A tutor appointed by the court is a dative tutor. A meeting of relatives must name a three-person tutorship council whatever the amount, and the Public Curator oversees all dative tutors; the insurance bond is required only above $25,000.

questions.q: Which tutors does Quebec's Public Curator oversee?
options: Only dative tutors managing property worth over $25,000
All legal tutors, and dative tutors managing over $25,000
Only tutors designated in a will by both of the parents
All dative tutors, and legal tutors managing over $25,000
questions.explain: The Public Curator oversees all dative tutors without exception and the legal tutors managing property worth more than $25,000. It audits their annual accounts and charges fees for its services to the minor's estate.

questions.q: Lucie and Hugo, both Quebec residents, marry during a trip to Mexico without a marriage contract and then return home. Which regime governs their property?
options: Mexico's default regime, since they married there
Partnership of acquests under the Civil Code of Quebec
Separation as to property, since they married abroad
No regime until the marriage is registered in Quebec
questions.explain: Their common domicile when they married was Quebec, so the Civil Code of Quebec governs their assets, as for Lise and Benoit, who married in Jamaica: they are under the legal regime, the partnership of acquests.

questions.q: Akira and Yumi married in Japan and moved to Quebec eight years later. They now separate. How are their assets handled?
options: The partnership of acquests applies, since they now live in Quebec
Japanese law governs everything, including the family residence
Japanese law sets their regime, but family patrimony applies first
Only assets acquired after their move to Quebec can be partitioned
questions.explain: Generally, the law where and when they married determines the matrimonial regime (as for Maria and Mario from Italy), but the Quebec family patrimony rules have priority and apply to all couples. An expert should be consulted in such cases.

questions.q: On their honeymoon, Maria signed a contract giving up any interest in the family home Manuel might buy. They married in Quebec without a marriage contract; the house is in Manuel's name. On divorce, what is the effect of her contract?
options: None; it is null, so the home's net value is split equally
It is valid, so Manuel keeps the full value of the house
It is valid only for assets bought after the honeymoon
It is valid unless she proves she signed under a threat
questions.explain: The house is the family residence acquired after the marriage, so its net value is split equally under family patrimony whatever the title. Family patrimony cannot be renounced during the marriage, so the honeymoon contract is null and void.

questions.q: Manuel, married in Quebec under the partnership of acquests, uses a van only in his plumbing business; it was paid half from his profits and half from his wife's salary. How is the van treated on their divorce?
options: Family patrimony, since both spouses paid for it
Excluded entirely, because it is a business asset
Manuel's private property, as the registered owner
Not family patrimony, but partitioned as an acquest
questions.explain: As a business asset, the van is not a family patrimony asset. But it was paid for from salary, which is an acquest, so the van is an acquest whose value is partitioned under the partnership of acquests.

questions.q: On a Quebec divorce, Henri's family patrimony assets are a $30,000 RRSP and furniture worth $15,000 bought on credit, with $15,000 still owing. His wife's net family patrimony value is $0. What must Henri pay her?
questions.explain: Henri's net value is $30,000 + $15,000 - $15,000 of debt = $30,000. The difference with his wife ($0) is $30,000, so he must transfer half, $15,000, in cash or property.

questions.q: Jeanne, married under the partnership of acquests, holds a $50,000 GIC: $20,000 was a gift from her mother, $20,000 she saved before the marriage and $10,000 she saved during it. On divorce, what part of the GIC is shared as acquests?
options: The full $50,000, as it is a financial asset
The $20,000 gift plus the $10,000 savings
Only the $10,000 saved during the marriage
None of it, since GICs are not family patrimony
questions.explain: A GIC is excluded from family patrimony, but the regime still applies: the $10,000 saved during the marriage is an acquest to be divided. Her pre-marriage savings and her mother's gift are not shared, as the course's answer shows.

questions.q: Rina owned a house when she married: worth $80,000, with a $60,000 mortgage (net value $20,000). It became the family residence and is now worth $200,000, fully paid. Using the course's formula, what increase in value does she deduct?
questions.explain: Deduction = net value at marriage x increase since marriage / gross value at marriage = $20,000 x $120,000 / $80,000 = $30,000. She also deducts the $20,000 net value, leaving $150,000 subject to partition.

questions.q: In the course's Dupuis example, the family patrimony value after deductions is $183,000 for Joseph and $20,000 for Marie. What must Joseph pay Marie to equalize?
questions.explain: The total family patrimony is $203,000, so each spouse is entitled to $101,500. Joseph holds $183,000 and must transfer $81,500 to Marie in cash or assets; $163,000 is the full difference, not half of it.

questions.q: In the Dupuis example, Joseph drives a leased minivan (residual value $18,900) that both spouses use. How is it treated in the partition?
options: Included in family patrimony at its $18,900 value
Not included, since he rents it rather than owns it
Included as an acquest at its residual value
Included because both spouses use the vehicle
questions.explain: Family patrimony includes vehicles used by the family that are owned by the spouses. Joseph rents the minivan, so it is not included in the assets to be partitioned.
